title: Infectious Disease in Plants
subtitle: Myrtle rust, Panama disease and the cost of a monoculture
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: assess the causes and effects of diseases on agricultural production, including but not limited to: plant diseases
classifying different pathogens that cause disease in plants and animals (ACSBL117)
Use examples to assess the effects of infectious diseases on plants
Conduct a scientific investigation to evaluate the effect of Panama disease on bananas
Explain the physical and chemical changes of a plant in response to the presence of pathogens
lessonIntent: Students can classify plant pathogens by type, assess the economic and ecological effects of plant disease using myrtle rust and Panama disease on bananas, and explain why low genetic diversity and biosecurity matter.
examSkill: Assess the causes and effects of a named plant disease, separating economic from ecological effects, and link a crop's genetic diversity to its vulnerability.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, infectious disease in plants. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: One nursery, then a whole continent
scenes.body: In 2010 myrtle rust was found at one NSW nursery. It has since spread across much of Australia, into hundreds of native species.
scenes.callout: How does one microscopic fungus outrun a continent?
scenes.caption: Myrtle rust spread from one NSW nursery to hundreds of native species across Australia.

voiceover.text: In April twenty ten, myrtle rust, a fungus called Austropuccinia psidii, was detected at a plant nursery on the Central Coast of New South Wales. Within about a year it had reached Queensland and Victoria, and it has since turned up in Tasmania, the Northern Territory and Western Australia. It now infects hundreds of native species in the myrtle family, including eucalypts, paperbarks, bottlebrushes and tea trees, and there's no cure. So how does one microscopic fungus spread across a continent? And what does plant disease really cost, on farms and in the bush? Let's dig in.

scenes.heading: Why plant disease matters
scenes.body: Plant disease does far more than dent yields, so you must assess both economic and ecological effects.

bullets.text: Plant pathogens cause roughly 10 to 16 percent of global crop losses every year.
They threaten Australian farm production and export markets worth billions.
They devastate native ecosystems, cascading into lost habitat and biodiversity.

scenes.secondary: Losing a dominant native species, as myrtle rust does to the myrtle family, alters soil chemistry, changes water cycles, and removes habitat for dependent animals.
scenes.callout: Always assess two things: the cause and the effects.
scenes.caption: Plant disease causes economic loss and ecological devastation, not just lower yield.

voiceover.text: Let's start with the scale, because the exam wants you to assess both causes and effects. Plant pathogens are responsible for roughly ten to sixteen percent of global crop losses every year, which is a direct threat to food security. In Australia, plant disease is one of the biggest ongoing threats to farm production and to our export markets. But here's the part students forget, the effects go well beyond the farm. When a disease removes a dominant native species, like myrtle rust is doing in the myrtle family, it cascades. Animals lose habitat and food, and biodiversity drops. So whenever you assess a plant disease, address the cause, which is the pathogen, and the effects, which are economic and ecological.

scenes.heading: The terms you need

bullets.text: Plant pathogen: a fungus, bacterium, virus or nematode that causes plant disease.
Biosecurity: measures that prevent the introduction and spread of pests and diseases.
Host resistance: a variety's ability to reduce infection or damage.
Monoculture: a large area planted with a single crop, often a single genetic variety.

scenes.callout: Biosecurity keeps the pathogen out; resistance limits the damage.
scenes.caption: Plant pathogen, biosecurity, host resistance, monoculture.

voiceover.text: Four terms before we go on. A plant pathogen is any agent that causes disease in plants, whether that's a fungus, a bacterium, a virus or a nematode worm. Biosecurity is the set of measures that prevent pests and diseases entering and spreading, and in Australia it starts right at the border. Host resistance is the ability of a plant variety to reduce the infection or damage a pathogen causes. And a monoculture is a large area planted with just one crop, often a single genetic variety. Keep that last one in mind, because genetic diversity is what decides how badly a disease can hit.

scenes.heading: Four plant pathogen types
scenes.body: Plant pathogens span four main groups, and each causes characteristic damage by a different mechanism.

bullets.text: Fungal: hyphae and enzymes, spread by spores, like myrtle rust and Panama disease.
Bacterial: enter via wounds and stomata, spread by water and tools, like crown gall.
Viral: replicate inside cells, spread by insect vectors, no cure once infected.

scenes.secondary: Nematodes are soil roundworms that feed on roots; root-knot nematodes cause galls that stunt the plant.
scenes.callout: Same pathogen families as animals, different species.
scenes.caption: Fungal, bacterial, viral, and nematode pathogens each damage plants differently.

voiceover.text: Now the pathogen types, and how they play out in plants. Fungal pathogens push hyphae into plant tissue and release enzymes that break down cell walls, and they mostly spread as spores in air, water or soil, like wheat stem rust, myrtle rust and Panama disease. Bacterial pathogens enter through wounds or stomata, then produce toxins or block the plant's vascular tissue, spreading via water, insects and contaminated tools, like crown gall. Viral pathogens replicate inside plant cells, spread mostly by insect vectors like aphids, and once a plant is infected there's no cure, banana bunchy top virus is an Australian example. And nematodes are soil roundworms that feed on roots, with root knot nematodes causing galls that stunt the whole plant.

scenes.heading: Economic and ecological effects
scenes.body: The damage runs from the visible symptom right through to lost markets and broken ecosystems.

bullets.text: Economic: reduced yield and quality, control costs, and lost export markets.
Ecological: loss of a dominant species, soil persistence, and altered habitat.
Many of Australia's worst plant diseases were introduced, not native.

scenes.secondary: Australia is free of some major plant diseases, such as fire blight of apples, and keeping them out protects both crops and export access.
scenes.callout: Prevention is far cheaper than cure.
scenes.caption: Plant disease causes economic losses and ecological damage; prevention beats cure.

voiceover.text: Now let's trace the chain from symptom to real world cost. On the economic side, you get reduced yield and reduced quality, where produce drops a grade or becomes unsaleable. Then there are control costs, like fungicides, resistant varieties, quarantine and replanting. And for an exporter, there's market access, because Australia is free of some major diseases, like fire blight of apples, and a detection could close overseas markets. On the ecological side, you can lose a dominant native species, pathogens can persist in soil for years, and habitats get altered. Here's the policy punchline. Many of Australia's most damaging plant diseases, like myrtle rust and banana bunchy top, were introduced from elsewhere, so preventing entry is far cheaper than managing a pathogen once it's established.

scenes.heading: Panama disease: a fungus in the xylem
scenes.body: Panama disease is Fusarium wilt of bananas, caused by the soil fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense.

bullets.text: Cause: a soil fungus that enters through the roots and grows in the xylem.
Effect: xylem blocked, so leaves yellow and wilt and the plant dies.
Spores survive in soil for decades, spread by soil, water, boots and machinery.
Cavendish plants are clones, so a whole plantation shares the same susceptibility.

scenes.secondary: The plant responds physically and chemically, plugging its xylem with tyloses and gums and making antifungal compounds, but in susceptible varieties this response is too slow.
scenes.callout: No genetic variation, no plants that survive.
scenes.caption: Fusarium wilt enters roots, blocks xylem and persists in soil; clonal Cavendish crops share one susceptibility.

voiceover.text: OK, now the example the new syllabus names, Panama disease of bananas, also called Fusarium wilt. It's caused by a soil fungus, Fusarium oxysporum, which enters through the roots and grows up inside the xylem. As it spreads, the xylem gets blocked, so water can't reach the leaves, and the plant yellows, wilts and eventually dies. The plant does respond, physically plugging its own xylem with growths called tyloses and gums, and chemically making antifungal compounds, but in susceptible varieties that response is too slow. Worse, the fungus leaves tough spores that survive in soil for decades, moving on muddy boots, machinery and water. And here's the biodiversity link. Almost every banana we eat is a Cavendish, and Cavendish plants are grown from suckers, so they're clones. A plantation has essentially no genetic variation, so if one plant is susceptible, they all are. There's history here too, because an earlier strain wiped out the Gros Michel banana in the twentieth century, and Cavendish replaced it.

scenes.heading: Assess Panama disease TR4
scenes.question: Panama disease Tropical Race 4 (TR4) infects Cavendish bananas and has no cure. It was found in the Northern Territory in 1997 and in Queensland's main growing region, Tully, in 2015. Assess its effects and evaluate how Australia manages it.
scenes.coachNote: Name the cause, split the effects into economic and ecological, then judge the management against the evidence.
steps: Cause: a soil fungus spread by contaminated soil, water, footwear, machinery and planting material.
Economic: infected plants destroyed, land unusable for Cavendish for decades, farm biosecurity costs.
Genetic and ecological: clonal Cavendish monoculture has no variation for resistance, so whole crops are exposed.
Management: quarantine infected farms, wash down vehicles and boots, plant disease-free plantlets, breed or engineer resistant bananas.
Evaluate: containment has slowed its spread, but with no cure, long-term security needs genetic resistance.
scenes.caption: TR4: soil-borne cause, economic and genetic effects, biosecurity slows it, resistance is the long-term fix.

voiceover.text: Let's assess Panama disease properly, the way an extended response demands. The strain that attacks Cavendish is called Tropical Race 4, or TR4. It was found in the Northern Territory in 1997, and in 2015 it reached Tully, in Queensland's main banana growing region. First, the cause, a soil fungus spread by anything that moves soil, including water, footwear, machinery and infected planting material. Next, the effects. Economically, infected plants have to be destroyed, the land can't grow Cavendish again for decades, and every farm carries extra biosecurity costs. Genetically and ecologically, a clonal monoculture has no variation for resistance, so whole crops are exposed at once. For management, infected farms are quarantined, vehicles and boots are washed down, growers plant disease free plantlets, and researchers are breeding and genetically engineering resistant bananas. So, evaluate. Strict containment has slowed its spread, but with no cure, the long term answer is genetic resistance.

scenes.heading: Two traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: thinking every plant disease can be cured with a spray. Plant viruses, and fungi hiding in the xylem and soil, cannot; control is prevention.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: thinking introduced pathogens are dangerous simply because they are foreign. The real reason is that native hosts have had no shared evolutionary history with them, so they carry no resistance.
scenes.callout: No cure for plant viruses; the danger is no shared history.
scenes.caption: Not every plant disease can be sprayed away; introduced pathogens are dangerous due to no co-evolution.

voiceover.text: Two traps to clear up. Trap one, thinking a plant disease can always be cured with the right spray. Plant viruses can't be cured at all, because they replicate inside the plant's own cells. And some fungi, like the one behind Panama disease, sit inside the xylem and survive in soil for decades, out of reach of sprays. For these, management is prevention, controlling vectors, using certified disease free planting material, and destroying infected plants. Trap two, assuming introduced pathogens are dangerous simply because they're foreign. They're dangerous because native hosts have had no shared evolutionary history with them, so they carry no built in resistance. So the danger isn't the pathogen's origin, it's the missing history, and low genetic diversity makes it worse.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A banana grower asks why Panama disease TR4 could destroy an entire Cavendish plantation, when a wild banana population might survive it. Explain, using genetic diversity.
answerSteps: Cavendish bananas are propagated vegetatively, so every plant in a plantation is a genetic clone.
Clones share the same alleles, so if one plant is susceptible to TR4, all of them are.
A wild population reproduces sexually, so it carries genetic variation.
Some wild individuals may carry alleles for resistance, survive and reproduce.
Answer: low genetic diversity leaves no resistant individuals, so the whole monoculture is vulnerable ✓
scenes.caption: Clonal Cavendish share one susceptibility; a genetically diverse population may include resistant survivors.

voiceover.text: Quick check. A banana grower asks why Panama disease could destroy an entire Cavendish plantation, when a wild banana population might survive it. Explain, using genetic diversity. Pause and reason it through. Right. Cavendish bananas are grown from suckers, so every plant in the plantation is a genetic clone, sharing the same alleles. If one plant is susceptible to TR4, they all are. A wild population reproduces sexually, so it carries genetic variation, and some individuals may carry alleles that give resistance. Those individuals survive and reproduce, so the population persists. So the answer is, low genetic diversity leaves no resistant individuals, which makes the whole monoculture vulnerable.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Plant disease causes 10 to 16 percent of global crop losses, plus ecological damage.
Four plant pathogen types: fungal, bacterial, viral and nematode.
Assess effects in two halves: economic and ecological.
Panama disease is a soil fungus that blocks banana xylem; clonal Cavendish crops have no resistance.
Introduced pathogens are dangerous because hosts have no co-evolved resistance; biosecurity keeps them out.
scenes.finalPrompt: Assessing a plant disease? Name the cause, split the effects into economic and ecological, and check the host's genetic diversity.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: scale, four types, two effect halves, Panama disease, co-evolution and biosecurity.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. First, plant disease causes roughly ten to sixteen percent of global crop losses each year, plus serious ecological damage beyond the farm. Second, there are four main plant pathogen types, fungal, bacterial, viral and nematode. Third, when you assess the effects, split them into economic and ecological. Fourth, Panama disease is a soil fungus that blocks banana xylem and lasts in soil for decades, and clonal Cavendish crops have no genetic variation to resist it. And fifth, introduced pathogens are so dangerous because native hosts have no shared evolutionary history with them, which is why biosecurity focuses on keeping them out. Next lesson, the same questions for animals. See you there.
